opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core challenge in robotics has always been what I call the data gap. Language models were trained on something like the equivalent of tens of thousands of human lifetimes of reading, all freely available on the internet. We just don't have anything comparable for robot motion. There's no internet of robot trajectories, of the forces at the fingertips, of what it actually feels like to pick up a glass or fold a shirt. So a lot of people look at that and say it'll take a hundred thousand years of robot data collection to catch up.

But here's what gives me some hope. When you look at images, the raw space is enormous. A modest image has millions of pixels, each with a range of values, so the number of possible images is astronomically large. Yet the images that actually occur in the world, the ones that matter, occupy a tiny sliver of that space. They have structure, regularities, edges, objects, lighting. And that's precisely why we've been able to compress them so effectively, and why generative models can learn to produce realistic images from what is, relatively speaking, a manageable amount of data.

The question is whether the same thing holds for robot motion. And I think there's good reason to believe it does. The space of all possible joint configurations and trajectories is vast, but the motions that are actually useful, reaching, grasping, pushing, wiping, live on something like a much lower-dimensional manifold. Humans don't explore every possible way to move their arm; we use a small set of motion primitives and combine them. If robot motions are similarly compressible, then the amount of data we need might be far less than the naive estimates suggest.

So that's the glimmer. It's not a guarantee. We don't yet know how compact those representations really are, especially once you factor in contact, friction, and all the messy physics of manipulation, which are notoriously hard to model. But if they are, then combining that with good old-fashioned engineering, physics models, simulation, and careful data collection could close the gap a lot faster than people fear. I'd just caution that it's going to be a steady climb rather than a sudden leap, and we should be honest about that.

r001.rationale: The response says images have structure and can be compressed, but does not say that recognizable semantic information survives substantial loss of image detail.

r002.rationale: It says useful robot motions may lie on a much lower-dimensional manifold and may be represented compactly.

r003.rationale: It links the lower-dimensional, compressible motion space to needing far less data than naive estimates suggest, conveying that fewer examples can cover the useful motions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that struck a lot of us in robotics is this question of why language models worked so well, and whether anything analogous could happen for robots. And one of the arguments that's been made, and I think it's a good one, is that language is actually a very compact representation. It's been compressed over thousands of years by humans into this discrete set of symbols, with a lot of structure, a lot of redundancy, and the internet gave us an enormous amount of it. So the models had something very learnable to chew on.

Now, when you look at robot motion, or images from a camera, it's a very different situation. The raw signal is enormously high dimensional. You've got millions of pixels per frame, you've got continuous joint positions, torques, contact forces, all changing over time. And the naive view is that you'd just need to collect a correspondingly gigantic amount of robot data to learn in that space, and we don't have it. We don't have an internet of robot motions. That's what I've called the hundred-thousand-year data gap.

But here's the glimmer of hope. There's good reason to believe that the actual information content of what a robot needs to perceive and do is much, much smaller than the raw data suggests. If you look at an image of a cluttered table, most of the pixels are redundant. What matters is a relatively small number of things: where the objects are, their shapes, which ones are graspable. And similarly with motion. Reaching over and picking up a cup is not fundamentally a million-dimensional problem. There's a low-dimensional manifold underneath. Humans do this effortlessly, and we don't do it by processing every pixel independently.

So if we can find representations that are compact, that capture that underlying structure, then suddenly the data requirements might shrink dramatically. You wouldn't need the hundred thousand years. You might get away with something that's within reach, especially if you combine real data with simulation and with the kind of structure we already know from geometry and physics. We've seen hints of this already. Latent representations in vision models, action tokenization, and some of the work on learning dynamics in a compressed space. None of it is solved yet, but it suggests the problem might be more tractable than the raw numbers imply.

And I'll be honest, I've been a skeptic about a lot of the hype in robotics. I don't think we're on the verge of general-purpose humanoids doing your laundry. But this particular idea, that the right representation could collapse the problem, that's one I genuinely find encouraging. It's the kind of thing that could change the slope of progress, not just extend the line.

r001.rationale: It says most image pixels are redundant and that a small set of meaningful features, such as object locations and shapes, matters, conveying that semantic information can remain despite omitting substantial image detail.

r002.rationale: It describes robot motion as having an underlying low-dimensional manifold and says compact representations could capture that structure.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says compact representations could make the data requirements shrink dramatically, linking a smaller representation to needing fewer examples.

astra-6.text:
Well, an image might have a million pixels, so at first glance you’re dealing with a million-dimensional space. But those pixels aren’t independent. There’s structure: objects, surfaces, edges. So there’s a possibility that the information you actually need can be captured in a much smaller representation.

And robot motions may have a similar property. Think about reaching for a cup. You could describe that as a long sequence of positions for every joint in your arm. But we don’t seem to think about it that way. There’s a coordinated motion, with variations depending on where the cup is and how it’s oriented. Perhaps that whole family of movements can be represented with relatively few parameters.

That’s the glimmer of hope: if we can discover those representations, learning and planning could become much more manageable. A robot wouldn’t have to learn every situation independently; it could use the underlying structure to generalise. That doesn’t solve robotics by itself, but it suggests that the apparent complexity of the problem may be much greater than the complexity we actually have to master.

r001.rationale: The response says image information may fit in a smaller representation, but does not say recognizable semantic information survives substantial loss of image detail.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a long sequence of joint positions with a family of coordinated movements that may be represented using relatively few parameters.

r003.rationale: It says structure could help robots generalize and avoid learning every situation independently, but does not explain that a smaller state space needs fewer examples for comparable coverage.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, an image might have millions of pixels, and a robot motion might involve a very long sequence of joint positions. If you treat all of those numbers as independent variables, the space you have to search is enormous. That’s one of the things that makes robotics so difficult.

But those variables aren’t independent. Images of the world have structure, and useful robot motions have structure. Think about reaching for a cup: there are many ways to do it, but they’re a tiny subset of all the possible movements your arm could make. So the hope is that we can find a much smaller set of variables that captures what matters.

If we can learn those representations, then learning and planning could become much more tractable. A robot might be able to generalise from a relatively small number of examples, rather than having to encounter every possible situation. That’s the glimmer of hope. It doesn’t solve the problem by itself, but it suggests that the apparent complexity of the problem may be much greater than its underlying complexity.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a long sequence of joint positions with a much smaller set of variables that captures what matters.
